newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Jewish leader slams Scientology letter.
newsitem.headline: German Jewish leader slams Scientology letter.

text.p: German Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis on Monday dismissed as "insulting" accusations from American celebrities that Germany has been oppressing Scientologists in the same way that Hitler persecuted Jews.

Speaking at a reception for his 70th birthday, Bubis told several hundred guests including Chancellor Helmut Kohl that such a charge was an affront to the memory of those who had perished and suffered in the Holocaust.
"It is insulting to the memory of the victims," said Bubis, who survived the Holocaust but whose father, brother and sister were killed in Nazi concentration camps.

The controversial letter that compared contemporary Germany with Nazi Germany was published as a full-page advertisement in the Paris-based International Herald Tribune newspaper last week. It was signed by Dustin Hoffman, Goldie Hawn, Oliver Stone, Gore Vidal and other entertainment figures.

Germany views the Church of Scientology as a threat to democracy. The federal and regional governments agreed last month to a series of steps to counter what they called the Scientologists' "expansionist aims and claim to domination".

The American celebrities, who said they were not Scientologists, said German efforts to limit the spread of the U.S.-based church group were "organised persecution" similar to that meted out to Jews in the 1930s. German politicians angrily rejected the charges made in the letter.

The celebrities' letter likened the Nazi book-burnings of the 1930s to a boycott called last year by the youth wing of Kohl's Christian Democrats against the 1996 Tom Cruise film "Mission Impossible" on the grounds that the actor was a Scientologist.
Johannes Gerster, a conservative political leader, said he had invited the celebrities to visit Germany in order to form a more objective view of the country.

"I hope they all come here to see Germany is a state based on the rule of law that respects pluralism," Gerster, leader of the Christian Democrats in Rhineland-Palatinate state. "I would love to meet them here to inform them about Germany."
Bubis said the letter, which was addressed to Kohl, did not take account of the changes that had taken place in German society since World War Two.
"I stayed because I discovered that another Germany had arisen," he said.
Kohl praised Bubis for explaining to the outside world that present-day Germany could not be compared to the Weimar Republic, whose collapse led to Hitler's National Socialists taking power in 1933.
At another birthday celebration in Berlin on Sunday attended by some 3,300 people, Bubis said that there still did not exist a "normal relationship" between Jews and non-Jews in Germany.
He said that right-wing extremism and neo-Nazism were in fact weaker in Germany than in many of its neighbours but that they tended to given more attention.

Sometimes criticised for taking too lenient a stance on the continuing implications for German society of the Holocaust, Bubis has nonetheless risked unpopularity by urging that Germans should not forget that period of their history.

Last week he criticised a long-delayed project to build a Holocaust memorial in Berlin, saying it was above all important that it be built despite disagreement by planners over what type of momunent they wanted.
